title: Tyr and the Binding of Fenrir
text:
In the Prose Edda, Snorri Sturluson tells how the gods raised the wolf Fenrir, a child of Loki, in their own home. He grew so fast and so fierce that only the god Tyr had the courage to go near him and feed him. Prophecies warned that the wolf would bring them ruin, so the gods decided to bind him.

Twice they brought chains, and twice Fenrir broke them with ease. Then dwarves made a fetter called Gleipnir from impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. It was as smooth and soft as a silk ribbon.

The gods brought Fenrir to an island and invited him to test his strength against it. The wolf suspected a trick. He would let them bind him only if one of the gods placed a hand in his mouth as a pledge that there was no deceit. The gods looked at each other. No one wanted to lose a hand. Then Tyr stepped forward and put his right hand between the wolf's jaws.

The gods bound Fenrir. The harder he struggled, the tighter Gleipnir held. All the gods laughed, except Tyr. He lost his hand.
lesson: When a plan requires someone to pay a personal price, the leader should be the one to offer. Trust is built by those who put themselves on the line, not by those who only make the plan.
